newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian, Belarus leaders to meet over union.
newsitem.headline: Russian, Belarus leaders to meet over union.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko were due to meet on Thursday to iron out differences over a controversial union deal one day before its planned signing.
Yeltsin and the hardline Belarus president, who signed a short and largely declarative union treaty last month, are expected to fill it out with a more detailed charter on Friday.
But with the rhetoric of integration running full steam ahead, both leaders appear at odds on the most important issues, including the powers of the future union and its ultimate aim.
Yeltsin said earlier this week that he saw Russia and Belarus merging into a single federation state at the end of the integration process, prompting angry reaction from his partner.
"Setting up a federation with Russia would be worse for Belarus than when it entered Stalin's Soviet Union," Lukashenko told reporters in his capital Minsk on Wednesday.
"We were not part of Russia under the Soviet Union," he added referring to the formally equal status Belarus shared with Russia and 13 other "union republics" in the communist empire.

A senior member of the Russian negotiating team, Sergei Shakhrai, has said that Minsk was strongly opposed to some Moscow ideas which could make the future union strong and binding on both sides. One proposal is for a single currency.
Belarus negotiators for their part seek the tight union of two independent states, each of whom would have equal rights.
Moscow is sceptical about this idea, stressing the difference in size and economic potential between the 150-million strong Russian federation and Belarus, which has 10 million people.
Vociferous nationalist opposition in Belarus has condemned the planned union as Moscow's plot to revive the empire and rob Minsk of its independence won in 1991.
Russian liberals bitterly oppose the union and say that a deal with Lukashenko could have a bad impact on Russian democracy and also could worsen Russia's image abroad.
But opinion polls show that the majority of the population in both states support the idea of close integration between the two former Soviet Slav republics.
For Lukashenko, whose authoritarian rule and poor human rights record had made Minsk a virtual pariah in Europe, union with Russia may mean the way out of international isolation.
The union, which would include privileged access to the Russian market and natural resources, also looks attractive for the crisis-stricken Belarus economy.
But Lukashenko appears not at all ready to sacrifice his sweeping powers won after he took his current post in 1994.

Some critics suggest that by forming a union with Moscow based on the principle "one country, one vote" Lukashenko hopes to break into the Russian political scene without surrendering any of his powers.
The Kremlin, alarmed by NATO's plans to expand eastwards, is keen to form a union with Belarus, whose position in Europe is strategically advantegeous and attractive for Moscow.
Russian natural gas pipelines running though Belarus to central and western Europe and a developed oil refining sector are another factor in favour of the union.

But Yeltsin made clear in a letter to Lukashenko earlier this year that Moscow, which has gone a long way on economic and political reforms, wants Minsk, where reforms are still at the embryonic stage, to play by its rules.
